rendered: The review does not recommend tens of nanometres for low-diffusivity oxides such as ZrO2. Its own diffusion-time calculation says that the ideal thickness for these surface coatings is thicknesses for these surface coatings should be below ten nanometers[1] for better electrochemical performance (see Fig. 10[2]). The tens-of-nanometres figure is what the literature usually reports, and the review attributes that to practical limits: The reported coating thickness in literature, in most cases, is in the[3] tens of nanometers as it is difficult to be controlled by easily scalable[4]. The reasoning for keeping coatings thin is as follows. Lithium diffusion through the coating takes longer as the layer gets thicker, and the most oxides and fluorides is extremely low, particularly for ZrO2[5], so the review notes that longer diffusion times are observed for thicker coating layers[6]. Because of this, the cost-effective, scalable coating materials with very low diffusivity are said to have a maximum recommended thickness of thicknesses are usually recommend to around ∼10 nm for effective[7]. A further reason is that ZrO2 is generally inert but may react with lithium ions and form secondary phases[8] (for example Li2ZrO3), which causes capacity fading. The review also observes that thicker-coated cathodes can still exhibit excellent rate capabilities despite the thickness of the[9] coatings, a behaviour it says is not clearly explained in the literature.
